approved: Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 - Second Reading - Amend donation laws

The majority voted in favour of agreeing with the main idea of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to [read the bill for a second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). The bill will now be considered in greater detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2021a/21bd011), the purpose of the bill was to implement a number of unrelated technical amendments, including to: * *clarify the operation of the public funding provisions where candidates for more than one party are in the same group on a Senate ballot paper (Senate groups)* * *replace the provisions relating to the interaction of state and federal political finance laws held to be invalid by the High Court of Australia in [Spence v Queensland](http://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/cases/cth/HCA/2019/15.html?context=1;query=2019%20hca%2015%20;mask_path=)* * *increase the flexibility of voting options to be offered to Australian voters in Antarctica and* * *introduce a number of technical amendments, some of which were previously proposed in the [Electoral Legislation Amendment (Modernisation and Other Measures) Bill 2018](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r6240) but removed prior to passage.*
Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 - in Committee - Lower disclosure threshold

The majority voted in favour of keeping sub-items (4) and (6) in item 34 of schedule 1 unchanged. In parliamentary jargon, they voted for them to *stand as printed*. This vote was put after Queensland Senator [Larissa Waters](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/queensland/larissa_waters) (Greens) introduced [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-09-02.263.1) to oppose those sub-items. After introducing her amendments, Senator Waters [said that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-09-02.263.1): > *Senator [Cormann](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/mathias_cormann) will be pleased to know that these amendments are the ones about indexation, so he can give us the spiel about how that's so very bad, which we all can't wait to hear. These amendments would remove indexation of the federal disclosure threshold. It started off at $13,200 and it's just progressively increased over the years. It's now up to $14,300. It makes a mockery of having a disclosure threshold. These amendments would say that you can't index the disclosure threshold. I commend them to the chamber.*

The majority voted against [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-09-02.265.1) introduced by Queensland Senator [Larissa Waters](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/queensland/larissa_waters) (Greens), which means they failed. Senator Waters [explained her amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-09-02.265.1): > *These amendments put beyond doubt that voter ID should not be a slippery slope towards voter ID at the polls. In dissenting reports to the 2016 JSCEM election review, both my party and the Labor Party noted that the government's claims of double voting and voter irregularity were actually not substantiated and were unsupported by the evidence. In Australia and internationally, the evidence supports the view that voter ID in fact suppresses and hinders citizen participation. Requiring voters to show formal identification documents risks disenfranchising First Nations people, family violence victims, young people without a driver's licence or homeless and itinerant people. The Electoral Commission has said that up to 1.5 per cent of new enrolments could be people without formal ID.* > > *I note that my home state of Queensland introduced voter ID laws before the 2015 election and, after a low voter turnout, the laws were repealed.* However, South Australian Senator [Don Farrell](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/don_farrell) (Labor) disagreed with the amendments, [arguing that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-09-02.267.1): > *Labor shares the concerns regarding the implementation of so-called voter ID laws and any amendments which would discourage voting and undermine our system of compulsory voting. We are assured, however—and we will be seeking further assurance from the Electoral Commissioner—that the amendments contained in the bill will not result in a polling official demanding identification. We therefore do not believe the change proposed by the Greens is necessary and
Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 - in Committee - Reform donation arrangements
Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 - in Committee - Restrict political donations

The majority voted in favour of passing the bill in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to [read the bill for a third time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). The bill will now be sent to the House of Representatives for their consideration. ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2021a/21bd011), the purpose of the bill was to implement a number of unrelated technical amendments, including to: * *clarify the operation of the public funding provisions where candidates for more than one party are in the same group on a Senate ballot paper (Senate groups)* * *replace the provisions relating to the interaction of state and federal political finance laws held to be invalid by the High Court of Australia in [Spence v Queensland](http://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/cases/cth/HCA/2019/15.html?context=1;query=2019%20hca%2015%20;mask_path=)* * *increase the flexibility of voting options to be offered to Australian voters in Antarctica and* * *introduce a number of technical amendments, some of which were previously proposed in the [Electoral Legislation Amendment (Modernisation and Other Measures) Bill 2018](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r6240) but removed prior to passage.*

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 was introduced, making technical amendments to the Commonwealth Electoral Act and Referendum Act, including narrowing federal donation rules following the High Court's decision in *Spence v State of Queensland*, allowing the Australian Electoral Commission greater workforce flexibility, and extending telephone voting to voters in Antarctica.

The Labor Party supported the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020, which makes technical amendments to the Commonwealth Electoral Act and Referendum Act, including clarifying federal-state donation disclosure rules after the High Court's Spence and Queensland decision, extending electronic voting to Antarctic workers, and requiring federal donations to be paid into dedicated federal accounts. Labor also secured a delayed commencement date of 1 December 2020 and reiterated its push for lowering the disclosure threshold to $1,000 and introducing real-time donation disclosure.

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 allows corporations to circumvent state donation laws by donating to federal parties, and the government is prioritising this over a national integrity commission, with Labor and the Liberals supporting the bill.

The speaker argued that the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 locks in the status quo on political donations and fails to address integrity reforms, contrasting it with their own Australian Federal Integrity Commission Bill which proposes a statutory review of political finance and lower disclosure thresholds. The speaker noted that federal donation disclosure thresholds remain at $14,300 with annual reporting, while states like New South Wales, Victoria, and Queensland require $1,000 thresholds and near real-time disclosure.

The speaker opposed the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 for weakening state and territory donation laws, arguing for a $1,000 disclosure threshold, real-time reporting, bans on gambling and tobacco donations, donation caps, and a federal integrity commission, citing James Packer’s $250,000 donation to Bob Katter and Crown’s nearly $2 million in donations as examples.

The speaker argued that the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 overrides state and territory laws requiring more transparent political donations, is supported by both major parties, and weakens democracy; they called for a federal integrity commission, truth in political advertising, and stronger donation disclosure laws.

The speaker argued that the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 would weaken state donation laws and make it easier for developers and big donors to funnel money to federal parties, citing $1.7 million in donations from Crown casino. They called for Canada-style donation rules—capping individual donations at Can$1,600, banning corporate and union donations, and requiring disclosure of donations over $200—to restore public trust.

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2020 makes housekeeping reforms to the Commonwealth Electoral Act, including extending confidential voting to Antarctic workers, removing unfit prepoll centres, and improving Senate ballot design and voter assistance for non-English speakers and people with disabilities.
